Copper Quarterly Report October 2008 # Chapter 3 The Supply/Demand Balance and Prices ## Key points - Copper has seen a spectacular reversal since hitting a new all time high in July. On the back of the financial crisis prices have plummeted below $4,000/t. However, this is due more to sentiment than current market conditions, with the fall in prices accompanied by a persistent cash to 3-month backwardation. - Both production and consumption forecasts have been lowered, but the supply response is not going to be enough to avoid a 1Mt deficit by 2010, with prices falling to average $1.80/lb and $1.68/lb in 2009 and 2010, respectively. - The market will adjust over 2011 and 2012 and move back into deficit in 2013, as demand recovers cyclically in industrialising countries. China in particular will move back into a double digit growth phase in 2010-2012. - The risks to the forecast are firmly on the downside, with the impact of the financial crisis on demand the biggest uncertainty. Therefore, we have outlined a downside alternative scenario, which is presented at the end of the medium term section. #### Copper prices succumb to financial meltdown 000t Cu

Recent trends ##### **Spectacular retreat from the July high as sentiment overwhelms fundamentals…** Since hitting a new high in July, copper prices have generally been heading in one direction, down. There had been an orderly retreat in the face of muted demand through August and into September. However, the retreat gathered pace in late September following the Lehman Brothers bankruptcy and Merrill Lynch selling itself to Bank of America over the weekend of 13-14 September. This precipitated the most acute stage of the previously slow burning financial crisis. Following the announcement of a bail out plan for the US banking system, copper on the LME attained a high of $7,322/t for 3-month material on 22 September. However, after Congress defeated the first bill authorising the bailout, copper prices went into headlong retreat. The sell off was broader than just in copper, as the credit markets seized up for all but overnight lending and banking shares plunged. Prices fell across all markets and asset classes, with the S&P index on the NY Stock Exchange down by 8.8% the day after the rejection of the bail out plan, its largest decline since the 1987 crash. The sell off gathered pace as many banks, investment funds and companies needing to generate cash dumped holdings for whatever they could get. Copper fell almost without a break to a low of $4,615/t on 10 October. This was followed by a volatile few days as the UK banking bailout plan spread across the world, with copper rising to a high of $5,606/t for 3-month on 14 October. Fears of a recession and th

e impact on metal demand pushed prices down again. A bout of dollar appreciation added more downward pressure as we went to press, pushing prices below the $4,000/t level. This latest appreciation in the dollar is being driven by several factors, including a proposed US fiscal boost, dollar repatriation by distressed US banks and companies, as well as cuts in European interest rates. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly Report October 2008 Chapter 3 101 ##### **…with stocks remaining thin on the ground, for now** The decline in market sentiment has overwhelmed the fundamentals. Exchange stocks have averaged just over 200,000t since 2006 and on 21st October stood a few hundred tonnes shy of 250,000t. An increase in inventory is not unusual in Q4, as consumers and merchants all seek to limit stock build ahead of the year end. Also, with the stocks-to-consumption ratio (reported stocks) at just over 2 weeks in Q3, there is not a lot of spare visible inventory around to immediately shift into exchange warehouses. However, these are not usual times and the deteriorating economic environment point to exchange stocks heading higher in the next few months. Most likely the build up in inventory will be concentrated in Europe and the US. This has been the case over the past few months, with contracted metal that is no longer required due to weak demand making its way into exchange warehouses. Asian exchanges have seen a modest reduction in total inventory since the end of July. SHFE stocks had fallen to a low of just 13,554t on 11th September, however they were back up to 34,790t by 16th October as Chinese restocking saw refined imports in September rise by about 30,000t. The SHFE-LME arbitrage moved decisively into positive territory beginning in early September and October should record another increase in imports, as domestic production growth slowed to just 4.5% year-on-year in September. ##### **Backwardation in cash-3m but a contango thereafter** Another major indicator of a tight of market is that nearby dates remain in backwardation. It took a decline to $4,500/t to shift the market into a contango of $20/t on 21 October. Up until then official prices had remained in backwardation albeit in a lower $0-100/t range versus $100200/t in July. The backwardation (tightness) is concentrated in November and implies that a short covering rally cannot be ruled out. However, longer term, prices approaching $4,000/t have led to the forward curve moving into a contango through to 63 months, where prices rise to just above $5,000/t. This is a dramatic change from the position even only one month ago (see chart), when the forward curve was in backwardation throughout and the 63 month price was over $6,000/t. When compared to two years ago, the 63 month price is over $1,000/t higher, indicating the increase in the market assessment of the underlying long run marginal cost of production. Even with a decline in input costs as a result of the economic slowdown, costs are likely to remain elevated above historical levels and keep the floor for copper prices higher than it has been in recent years. ional Limited confidential 104 Copper Quarterly Report October 2008 Chapter 3 ##### **Demand growth slowing in most markets…** The demand picture has been deteriorating since the beginning of 2008, as the bursting of the US sub-prime bubble in August 2007 played itself out. Concerns about consumption had increased as the Chinese government‟s policy to tame inflation saw Chinese refined demand slow to 5.2% this year from 16.1% in 2007. The financial crisis in the mature industrialised markets is accelerating and is amplifying the slowdown in demand that was already evident. This combination has led to sharply reduced refined demand growth forecasts compared to earlier in the year, with 2008 now forecast at just 1.5%. This is compared to the view in April this year, when we had 2008 growth at 3.7%. ### Consumption forecast for 2008 cut by 2.6% and 2009 by 5.4% since April Actual and forecast consumption, 2000-09 20000

##### **…with spot premia slipping to reflect the poor state of demand…** The deteriorating demand picture is reflected in the market premia. The financial turmoil effectively saw the Q3 lull in spot market activity extended into Q4, with very little spot material traded anywhere in industrialised markets. Only the hotspots of the Middle East and China have seen any interest. As a result, the premia range widened at the lower end as Q3 progressed, to 5-7¢/lb in the US and $30-70/t in Europe. It appears that the physical market was broadly in balance in Q3, with semis producers requirements met from contracted tonnages. A further sign of the slow market is that Chilean tenders have been coming in progressively lower throughout 2008 in response to both demand for metal but also falling freight rates. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly Report October 2008 Chapter 3 105 Data: CRU, *All prices are for LME Grade A cathode, basis M+1, cif parity Rotterdam, CAD © 2008 CRU International Limited confidential ##### **…but supply delays mount** The credit crunch is seeing the outlook for supply deteriorate alongside demand, particularly at the mine level. The lack of lending and falling prices are combining to see cash poor miners facing liquidity problems. There have already been reports of late stage projects halted in the face of uncertainty over their access to capital. Vulcan Resources and Asian Minerals halted work on the Kylylahti nickel-copper-cobalt in Finland and Ban Phuc nickel-copper project in Viet Nam, respectively in September. Mwana Africa also announced on 22 October that it is scaling back exploration activity to conser

ve cash in a bid to survive the next 12 months. 

Underperformance at the existing mines continued over the past three month, with Escondida suffering a SAG mill failure in October on top of a reduction to output due to lower head grades this year.  This combined with other disruptions means that Escondida‟s mine production in 2008 will be 230,000t below 2007 levels.  In addition, delays to Codelco‟s mill expansions that were meant to counteract declining headgrades will hold back the company‟s production. Grasberg also suffered a pit wall failure that will defer 68,000t of H2 production to future periods.  Even strikes have made a come back, with Xstrata‟s Kidd Creek operations strike bound and KGHM facing a one day strike on 5<sup>th</sup> November.

## 3. Short term market outlook 

The changes in the economic outlook have been marked since the last Quarterly.  As the financial crisis unravelled the historical parallels used to compare this slowdown have shifted back in time to the 1970s and 1930s, rather than the 1980s and 1990s.  However, the comparisons to the 1930s are looking overblown as the global and coordinated response to the crisis is turning what could have been a slide into depression into an old fashioned boom-and-bust recession, as the leveraging (debt) that drove the boom turns into the deleveraging (debt repayment) that is driving the bust. As a result, the speed of the adjustment is difficult to predict with any precision and the risks at present are all on the down side.  Therefore, we have included an alternative scenario in which demand falls more than in the base case, and which is discussed later in the chapter. 

The scale of the crisis in the financial sector (which has also drawn in authorities in South East Asia as well as Switzerland and Australia) suggests that the de-leveraging process and counterparty risk concerns will quickly spread from financial markets to companies operating in the physical refined, scrap and concentrate markets.  A considerably weaker demand environment and tighter credit markets will undermine companies‟ ability to secure and/or refinance working capital loans or suitable letters of credit to back (foreign) trade.  In addition, suppliers fulfilling orders will be sensitive to the risk of increased payment delays and/or default, and are likely to press for full advance payment settlement in some regions – which would put even long-standing business relationships under strain.  Financing of metal stocks will also come under increased scrutiny.  Against this backdrop of dwindling demand and the tighter credit environment, we would not be surprised to see a continued build up in exchange inventory as contracted tonnages arrive but there are no longer the orders to match.  It remains to be seen how quickly exchange inventory builds, given recent events.

CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly Report October 2008 Chapter 3 107 ##### **Race to the bottom in 2009-10: Demand in the lead…** As the outlook has worsened the race to the bottom is on between supply and demand, with demand ahead of the game at the moment. The consumer reaction to the credit crunch is only becoming evident in mature industrialised markets, with the full effects on employment outside the financial sector only likely to manifest themselves in the next few months. News flow, and therefore sentiment, will only get worse in the short term, accelerating the downward spiral. We expect copper consumers to live hand-to-mouth well into 2009 and we understand that contract negotiations have been pushed onto the back burner for the time being. Consumers will be unwilling to commit to long term contracts until the depth of the economic slowdown becomes clearer. They will rein in their contracted volumes to below levels considered normal only a couple of months ago and counterparty risk will remain a major issue. ### 2008 contract premiums well above spot and $80/t in 2009 would likely keep it that way Chilean cathode* tenders, 2007-2009 Jan-07 Feb-07 Apr-07 Sep-07 Jan-08 Feb-08 Mar-08 May-08 Jul-08 Jan-09
We forecast that world consumption will grow by just 1.9% in 2009, following the 1.5% growth in 2008. This outturn comes from steady growth in the developing world of 6.6%, with China up by 5.5% while demand in other developing countries increases by 7.8%. This growth is offset by a second year of decline in consumption in the mature industrialised markets of just over 3%. In 2010, global consumption is forecast to pick up to 5.1%, as China‟s cyclical slowdown is reversed and refined demand there rises back to 11.5%. The rest of the developing world will see growth of 6.9%, while demand from the mature industrialised countries themselves will remain flat relative to 2009 levels. ##### **…but production will catch up** The producers have already announced their intention to review production plans, with exploration and expansion projects throughout the copper production cycle already being curtailed and significant industry rationalisations likely to take place. Producers will reduce their exposure very quickly to maximise their chance of surviving the downturn and to CRU International Limited confidential 108 Copper Quarterly Report October 2008 Chapter 3 participate in the up turn when it comes. Higher cost and/or highly leveraged operations will be subject to increased risk of closure or acquisition by better capitalised companies with stronger net cashflow positions. With credit difficult to obtain (except p

ossibly from national governments or other friendly lenders), mines will not be in a position to extend the life of a loss-making operation.  Therefore, the supply response in the short run is likely to be much faster than in previous downturns. 

Given the timing of the publication of this report, we have not had time to fully assess which particular operations will be hit by financing and/or refinancing delays.  Therefore, we have accounted for such disruptions by a bottom line “credit crunch delays” adjustment.  These will take the form of further announcements such as by Freeport McMoRan that it would stop capital investment at its Bagdad, Miami and Sierrita mines in the USA and Rio Tinto‟s change of tack on their bullish views of the demand for copper, which casts doubts over the potential development of some of their projects. 

It is important to note that the “credit crunch delays” are on top of our usual disruption allowance.  The copper market has suffered from five years of “unexpectedly” high disruptions to output.  This underperformance due to technical, labour and political risk is not likely to change just because we have entered a downturn in the market.  For example, next year sees labour contracts at 3.0Mt of mine capacity up for renewal.  The potential for strikes next year may come from the prevention of reduction in staffing and other cost saving measures. Therefore, we have maintained our relatively high disruption allowance. 

We now forecast refined production will rise by 4.4% in 2009.  This includes a bottom line 12,000t reduction to account for the beginning of delays to junior and mid-tier projects in the face of financing difficulties as a result of the credit crunch.  In addition, production capacity increases of almost 900,000t in 2008 will still feed through to boost overall output.  In 2010, production is forecast to increase by 8.2%, or 1.6Mt, despite a further 102,000t reduction in credit crunch delays.  The jump in 2010 is explained in part by the ramp up of several new projects which total over 240,000t.  In addition, Escondida is expected to raise production by 260,000t compared to 2009, as the SAG mill failure is rectified and mill expansions are brought on line to increase ore throughput in order to overcome declining head grades.  The balance of the increase comes from brownfield expansions and other incremental increases in production at existing mines. 

##### **Prices heading below $2.00/lb** 

Given the sharp deterioration in demand, the supply demand/balance in the very near term is set to balloon to almost 300,000t in Q4 2008, taking the annual figure into a solid 267,000t surplus instead of the 154,000t deficit we expected three months ago.  As sentiment deteriorates throughout the quarter, we now forecast that prices will average just $2.0/lb in Q4. 

In 2009 we expect a surplus of 694,000t, which rises to just over 1.0Mt in 2010.  A surplus of over 1.0Mt previously materialised in 2001, and prices

averaged 72¢/lb ($1,558/t), down from 82¢/lb ($1,814/t) on average in 2000. This time around, prices are not expected to plumb to these depths as the rise in production costs since 2002 has raised the threshold at which mines will embark on cutbacks. Prices will fall to an average of $1.80/lb ($3,975/t) in 2009. As the build up in stocks continues, prices will fall further to average $1.68/lb ($3,700/t) in 2010. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly Report October 2008 Chapter 3 109 The recent shift in the Chinese government‟s economic policy from containing inflation to promoting economic growth will support the infrastructure build in the country. China will need metal no matter what. However, the SRB policy on stock rebuilding remains a major wild card for the copper market. We understand the SRB in China is contemplating buying significant tonnages of copper. We expect that the SRB will look to come into the market once prices bottom out. This leaves the main unanswered question being what price will trigger the SRB to make a move and whether they will look to buy in bulk or build up stocks relatively gradually over a few quarters. markets to be over and these markets to be in recovery mode.  Due to its relative isolation, except through trade impacts, Chinese demand will accelerate to peak at 15% in 2011 before easing back to grow by 9.0% in 2013.  With a cyclical recovery in other emerging markets and modest growth in the mature markets, global consumption growth will rise to peak in 2012 at 6.0%. 

Despite the implosion of prices, substitution will remain a significant threat to copper demand in the medium term.  Differentials with competing materials will not go back to the levels of the early 2000s when copper averaged $250/t higher than aluminium for example.  In fact, the downturn will increase pressure to switch to cheaper materials, less volatile commodities and away from copper.  There is a concerted effort by the US air conditioner industry to look at switching to aluminium rather than copper tube.  Aluminium also continues to pose a threat in the winding wire and heat exchanger markets. 

On the production side, the credit crunch delays will peak in 2011 at 314,000t and help rein in production growth to just 2.9%, with a risk that low prices and tight credit availability will result in more cutbacks of production than we have forecast.  However, in the base case the market will remain in surplus in 2012 and inventory levels will hit their maximum levels in this cycle.  Prices will begin to pick up in 2011 and rise modestly in 2012.  The build up in demand and the hiatus of projects in the previous three years will mean that by 2013 the market will be back in deficit and face a return to tighter conditions in the years beyond the current outlook period.  As a result, we forecast that prices in 2013 will rise to an average of $2.10/lb. 

##### **Alternative scenario – Demand shock** 

Unlike three months ago, the biggest relative downside risks have shifted from supply towards demand.  We have run an alternative scenario in which the impact of the slowdown in economic activity in mature markets is more severe than in the base case but also recovers more quickly. In this scenario, demand for copper falls by 3.5% in 2009.  In North America, Western Europe and Japan consumption falls by 9.5%, comparable to 2001 when demand fell by 11.5%.  China sees a higher negative impact on exports that reduces growth to just 4%.  The supply response is quicker than in the base case, with cutbacks of almost 400,000t of committed production in 2009, but this is still insufficient to avoid a surplus of over 1Mt. 

Under this alternative scenario, global refined consumption growth begins to recover in 2010, rising by 2.4%.  Supply cutbacks of over 2Mt/y in 2010 compared to the base case lead to a 1.0% decline in output and a surplus in 2010 of about 400,000t.  Supply begins to recover in 2011.  Demand picks up strongly in 2011 as well, led by China bouncing back to grow strongly. As a result, the market goes from balanced in 2010 back into a deficit of almost 500,000t in 2011.  The r

elatively strong cyclical demand recovery continues throughout the remainder of the outlook period. However, the supply side finds it difficult to match demand growth and by 2013 we are back to declining inventories and prices head higher. As the heat chart below shows all the LME metals are looking to move into surplus territory amid the deteriorating demand environment. © 2008 CRU International Limited confidential ##### **All losers – but to what degree** The financial crisis has already taken its toll on all the LME traded metals as the markets react to the anticipated downturn in consumption and a strengthening dollar. All the metals prices have tumbled in recent weeks although as the chart below outlines, nickel prices have suffered the largest decline, slumping 60% since the start of this year. Sentiment in the base metals remains weak due to the ongoing demand fears, and history tells us that prices in a recession can fall well below the level where high cost producers fail to cover their costs. ##### **Aluminium – surpluses looming** What is surprising is that the aluminium prices have declined the least – just 10% - since the beginning of the year. We must assume that the market has already factored in the looming surpluses currently forecast in the market. Aluminium producers are now facing tough decisions as metal prices have fallen below cost support levels. With demand forecasts being CRU International Limited confidential 116 Copper Quarterly Report October 2008 Chapter 3 downgraded and metal surpluses building, this is likely in CRU‟s view to lead to curtailments of capacity in the market. With most smelters in China losing money at current metal prices, CRU expects Chinese producers to cut output and delay some of the planned expansion projects. LME stock levels have continued to increase at US warehouses t

hroughout the past month. 

The fall in prices means that aluminium prices are now well below the cost support level of not just smelters operating at the top of the business operating costs curve.  At current LME prices, 33% of global smelters are operating with costs above a price of US$2,275/t, which accounts for a tonnage of 13.6Mt/y.  China accounts for 10.8Mt/y of this total.  This means that 75% of Chinese smelters are losing money at current LME prices and on a SHFE price basis this rises to over 93%.  In the current climate of a market surplus and a weakening demand outlook this places producers under tremendous strain to delay ramp-up projects, cut back production or even close operations at current cost and price levels.

##### **Tin – a major reversal around the turn of the year** 

The tin price has dropped by more than 50% from its mid-May peak and by 20% since the start of the year.  CRU argued that tin was over-valued back in May as a result of fund activity and we believe that it looks distinctly under-valued now.  Speculative short-selling in the last few weeks is either purely technically driven or reflects the idea that a global recession will result in a major fall in metals demand in 2009.  But in the case of tin, supply is falling faster than demand.  In particular we estimate that Indonesian mine production will be 22% lower in 2008 than last year, and 41% down on its 2005 peak.  There is an estimated supply shortfall of around 20,000t this year which is unlikely to be eliminated in 2009.  The announced closure of the Indonesian private smelters is part of a wider picture of supply problems.  We see a sharp bounce back in prices and/or a significant widening of the LME backwardation, probably around the turn of the year.

##### **Lead – loses more than half its value since Q1 2008** 

LME lead prices have already fallen a long way, with 3-months official prices more than halving in value since the high of $3461/t in March.  Prices have been trading in a sideways range since the early summer.  However, it is a sign of how volatile lead trading has become when such sideways trading has been in such a wide near-$800/t range ($1,525 to $2,310/t since mid-May).  In September, the LME 3-month lead price averaged $1,882/t (85¢/lb), the fourth successive monthly average below $2,000/t (91¢/lb).  More interestingly, the monthly trading range has narrowed in each of the last three months - $665/t in July (high-low range), $450/t in August and $239/t in September.  Like copper, lead's rate of descent has increased recently, causing some concern.  As soon as support at $1,950/t was breached, volatility increased and the

market, which was already oversold, became critically so.  Lead prices have been somewhat becalmed in the eye of the financial storm, drifting (rather than diving) lower in the last week or so.  However, the consequent hit on the already darkening picture of metals demand with a disappointing post-summer demand pick-up on both sides of the Atlantic is now commanding the market‟s full attention.  The Chinese prognosis is even more crucial to health of demand, given that it now accounts for about one third of the world total.  However for the moment, Chinese lead demand is reported to remain reasonably buoyant and for now, news of any primary supply cuts or shortfalls has been relegated to the sidelines. 

##### **Zinc – below the average producer’s operating costs** 

Amid the meltdown in the financial markets, zinc prices have continued to plummet.  LME 3- month zinc prices have lost around 47% of their value since the beginning of this year and around 30% since the end of September alone.  For some metals, these corrections were long overdue and have just removed an irrational froth.  However, zinc‟s fall has driven prices to unsustainable lows.  Following what had already been a significant erosion since its late-2006 peak, zinc‟s price is now so low that even the average producer cannot cover its operating costs. This will not last.  Some swinging cutbacks will be forced.  However, we would not bet against prices falling further before producers have time to react.  Even before the onset of the financial crisis and the meltdown of confidence in the banking sector, zinc consumption had been significantly undermined by the deterioration in North America and Europe‟s main end-use sectors.  This raises the question of how much global demand destruction there is realistically left for zinc.  We think not very much more, assuming the worst of the credit crisis has passed. In the mean time, further closures or production cutbacks among zinc mines and smelters are inevitable, simply through the establishment of a new much lower trading range for zinc prices which has cut even further into the cost curve.  Although all economic logic suggests that prices have already fallen far too far this does not mean that that market no longer has any downside risk.  In this respect, we are not surprised by the results of Macquarie‟s LME Week survey which showed that, over the next year, zinc is the least favoured LME metal for both long and short speculation. 

##### **Nickel – prices tumble to 3-year low amid financial turmoil** 

LME nickel prices have slumped by over 35% since the end of September as the global financial crisis has raised fears that a severe economic recession is imminent.  Even government efforts to shore up the banking system have done little to boost confidence and staunch the downward trend in nickel prices which have fallen by to close to $10,500/t on a 3-month basis. Such developments could not have come at a worse time.  Already sufferi

Indeed, October is now being singled out as potentially one of the worst months for stainless output this year. Since LME nickel prices are already trading at levels below the marginal costs of production, the best case scenario facing this market is that sizeable cutbacks to nickel output will emerge quickly. Gold and silver by-product revenue has also increased but nothing like that of sulphuric acid. On the other hand, they are not expected to fall back as far sulphuric acid, either. By 2007, the price of gold had risen by 157% on 2001 lows and silver by 206%. The forecast for this year is for a 32% rise in the annual average price of gold to $917/oz. and silver a 20% rise to $16/oz. These higher prices translate into higher smelter revenues through a revenue sharing formula between the miners and the smelters. In Japan, this translates into net revenue for the smelters ranging from 0.6¢/lb for concentrates from Mantos Blancos to 5.1¢/lb for those from Telfer. Silver is not so important in Japan, with most mine‟s concentrate attracting only 0.1¢/lb in revenue, with the exception of the El Teniente and Cerro Verde, which attract 1.9¢/lb and 2.5¢/lb respectively. In Europe, silver by-product revenues are much higher than in Japan, while gold is comparable. Gold revenue in Europe ranges from 0.6-4.7¢/lb but silver 1.92.9¢/lb. Therefore, by-product revenues from gold will continue to escalate over the next two years before declining, while silver revenues will fall from next year. ##### **The view from CRU’s Price Risk Management** In September, the LME Cash price averaged $6,986/t, approximately $650/tonne below the August monthly average and the second consecutive month of sharp declines. This was du

e to almost all of the components of the price moving negatively.  The only component that rose was the Chinese trade component.  CTAs moved their average position to net short in September deducting $50/tonne to the price m/m.  Hedge funds saw the largest decline this month as that component fell by $350/tonne, as the credit crunch and financial turmoil led to a requirement for some fund liquidation.  This was further supported by growing fears about weaker global demand and consequently a significant surplus in 2009.  CRU‟s Price Risk Management practice estimates the overall funds influence upon copper price to have declined from around $1,875/t (~22% of the $8,413/t average cash price) in July to just $1,025/t in September (~15% of the $6,986/t average cash price).  Index fund participation in the copper market has continued to decrease since last month‟s publication.  The tightness in credit markets has forced investors to continue to deleverage positions both long and short.  The current situation is expected to persist for the next several months, providing reason to believe the outflow of index fund money is likely to continue.  In fact at the time of writing we calculate that the total fund affect on the copper price is now $2000/MT less than it was just three months ago and also net short!
